summary: For 6–7 year-olds, teach communication with light or sound as a design-build-test-improve engineering task: the child defines a real problem (send a message to a friend across a distance who can't hear them), plans and physically builds a device (cup-and-string telephone for sound, a torch signaller for light, or a drum for a beat pattern), agrees a shared CODE with the receiver so the device carries real information, then tests it over a measured distance and improves it. The big idea is that communication is information transfer — not merely making light or noise. The underlying physics (why light or sound carries the signal) is deferred to later years and need not be explained here.
misconceptions: Thinking the device just needs to make light or sound, rather than carry an AGREED message over the distance — communication is information transfer, not mere output.
Treating design as one-shot ('I built it, I'm done') instead of an iterative test-and-improve process.
Believing a string telephone works best SLACK — in fact the string must be taut to carry the vibration; a loose string kills the signal.
Assuming a louder or brighter device is automatically 'better', rather than testing whether the message actually gets across clearly at the far end.
Confusing 'communicating' with just making a noise or shining a light at someone — with no shared code, no information is sent.

activities.title: Build and test a real signal device over a distance
steps: Name the problem out loud: 'I need to send a message to a friend who is across the room and can't hear me speak.'
Sketch or describe a plan for a device before building it — choose light (a torch signaller), or sound (a cup-and-string telephone or a drum beat pattern).
Build the device from real tools and materials.
Agree a simple shared code with your partner BEFORE sending, e.g. one flash = 'yes', two flashes = 'no', or a drumbeat pattern for an agreed word.
Send the message and check with your partner whether they received the intended meaning correctly.

If it fails, work out WHY before changing something: if the meaning was wrong, fix or clarify the agreed code; if the signal could not be seen or heard at all (e.g. a slack string, or a flash too dim across a wide, bright room), pull the string taut, make the flash brighter, or shorten the gap.
Measure how far apart you can stand and still have the message arrive correctly.
Build or test a second device and compare the two: which carries the message further, and what are the strengths and weaknesses of each?
activities.insight: A device communicates only when an agreed code AND a well-built device work together to carry a real message over the distance — communication is sending information, not just producing light or noise.

activities.title: Define and brainstorm the problem with an inventor
steps: Take on a real scenario: an inventor needs to signal a ship at sea, or send a message to a friend across a valley.
Answer the inventor's questions: What problem are we solving? Who needs to receive the message, and why can't we just walk over or shout?
Brainstorm ways light or sound could carry the message — flashes, drumbeats, a string line between two cups.
Answer the pushback: 'How will they know what your flash MEANS?' — propose a code.
Hand off your best idea to the building stage and actually make it.
activities.insight: Good design starts by clearly defining the problem and the audience, and by planning how the signal will carry a meaning — not just how to make a signal.

activities.title: Explore real communication devices and their codes
steps: Look at real communication devices one at a time: cup-and-string telephone, lighthouse, drum, semaphore flags, bell.
For each, work out how it sends a signal far away and what 'code' it uses — flashes, beats, flag positions, rings.
Play a 'what message is this sending?' guessing game for a given signal.
Use the examples to spark ideas for your own device and code.
activities.insight: People across history use many different devices to send information over distance, and each relies on an agreed code — giving ideas for your own design.

activities.title: Quick check on design steps and signal types
steps: Put the design steps in order: define → plan → build → test → improve.
Sort devices into 'uses light' versus 'uses sound'.
Answer: 'What makes a string telephone work — a taut string or a slack string?' (Correct answer: taut.)
activities.insight: The design process has a usual working order and is iterative (you loop back to improve), and different devices rely on light or on sound to carry a signal.

checkQuestion: Your job: send a short secret message to a friend across the room without speaking or walking over. Using a torch (or a cup-and-string phone), design a way to do it, agree with your friend how it works, then send the message and see if they get it right. If it doesn't work, change something and try again.
checkAnswer: The child designs a device/method AND agrees a shared CODE with the partner (e.g. one flash = yes, two = no; or taps for letters), keeps a cup-string phone TAUT, sends the message, checks whether the partner decodes it correctly, and — if it fails — diagnoses why and changes something before retrying. Success = the friend correctly receives the intended message.
